text: The Kubernetes course taught you that the scheduler places pods based on declared CPU and memory requests — resources Kubernetes understands natively. GPUs aren't part of that built-in model at all. A node with eight physical GPUs attached looks exactly like a zero-GPU node to the scheduler, until something tells Kubernetes those GPUs exist, and that's the gap this lesson closes, building directly on the resource-request model from the Kubernetes course.

That something is the device plugin framework, a generic Kubernetes mechanism for vendor-specific code to discover specialized hardware and advertise it as an extended resource. NVIDIA's implementation runs as a DaemonSet, one pod per GPU node, discovering the GPUs there and reporting them to the kubelet as nvidia.com/gpu. Confirm it worked with kubectl describe node, checking Capacity and Allocatable for that resource.

The device plugin itself assumes the driver and container toolkit from the last lesson are already installed — it doesn't install them. In production, the NVIDIA GPU Operator usually handles all of it together, driver, toolkit, and device plugin, across a whole node pool through one Helm chart rather than configuring each node by hand.

Requesting the GPU in a pod spec looks exactly like requesting CPU or memory — same resources block, same mental model you already built in the Kubernetes course. Two differences matter here: nvidia.com/gpu only makes sense under limits, with requests forced equal to limits, and by default it's allocated as a whole integer, so a pod asking for one GPU gets exclusive use of an entire physical card, never a fraction of one.

A node taint paired with a pod's nodeSelector is what keeps that expensive hardware honest — the selector pulls GPU-needing pods onto GPU nodes, while the taint actively keeps everything else off, since a selector alone never stops an unrelated pod from landing there too. Next lesson tackles the flip side of 'whole integer only': sharing one physical GPU across multiple workloads without wasting most of its idle capacity.
